content: Heavy menstrual bleeding can significantly affect the quality of life in otherwise healthy women. The perception of what constitutes heavy menstrual bleeding is subjective, and treatment decisions are often based on the individual’s tolerance of symptoms. Surgical options for managing heavy menstrual bleeding include conservative procedures such as uterine resection or ablation, as well as hysterectomy. Medical treatments include oral medications and the use of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (LNG-IUS). The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of surgical interventions versus medical therapies for heavy menstrual bleeding. A systematic search of multiple databases, including Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and clinical trial registries, was conducted up to January 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing conservative surgery or hysterectomy with medical treatments (oral or intrauterine) were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for bias, extracted data, and analyzed the results. The primary outcomes evaluated were menstrual bleeding, satisfaction rates, and adverse events. Data were pooled where appropriate, and the quality of evidence was assessed using GRADE methodology. Fifteen RCTs involving 1,289 women were included in the analysis. Surgical interventions studied included hysterectomy and endometrial resection or ablation, while medical interventions included oral medications and LNG-IUS. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations such as lack of blinding, attrition, and imprecision. Long-term findings were challenging to interpret due to a high proportion of women in the medical treatment groups eventually undergoing surgery. Surgery versus Oral Medication: Endometrial resection was more effective than oral medication in controlling bleeding at four months (RR 2.66, 95% CI 1.94 to 3.64, moderate-quality evidence) and at two years (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.57, low-quality evidence). However, no significant difference was observed at five years (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.34, very low-quality evidence). Satisfaction rates were higher in the surgical group at two years (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.74, moderate-quality evidence), but no difference was noted at five years (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.37, very low-quality evidence). Adverse events were less frequent in the surgical group at four months (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.46). However, 59% of women in the oral medication group underwent surgery within two years, and 77% within five years, complicating long-term comparisons. Surgery versus LNG-IUS: Hysterectomy provided better objective control of bleeding at one year compared to LNG-IUS (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.19, moderate-quality evidence). However, no significant difference in quality of life was observed between the groups at five or ten years. By ten years, 46% of women initially assigned to LNG-IUS had undergone hysterectomy. Adverse effects of hysterectomy included surgical complications such as bladder or bowel perforation and vesicovaginal fistula. LNG-IUS was associated with ongoing bleeding and hormonal side effects. When conservative surgery was compared to LNG-IUS, the surgical group had better subjective control of bleeding at one year (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.32, low-quality evidence). Satisfaction rates were higher in the surgical group at one year (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.28), but this finding was sensitive to the statistical model used. No difference in satisfaction rates was observed at two years (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.08). Adverse events, such as bleeding and spotting, were less frequent in the surgical group at one year (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.82, moderate-quality evidence). Long-term data on the proportion of women in the LNG-IUS group who eventually underwent surgery were limited. Conclusions: Surgical interventions, particularly hysterectomy, are more effective than medical treatments in reducing menstrual bleeding at one year. However, hysterectomy carries a risk of serious complications, and less invasive treatments should be considered as first-line options. LNG-IUS and conservative surgery are both effective, safe, and acceptable alternatives. Oral medications are less suitable for long-term management, while LNG-IUS offers a viable non-surgical option for most women.
